title: Vance Just Launched the Biggest H-1B Fraud Probe in History. For 600,000 Indian Visa Holders, the Ground Just Shifted.
excerpt: The vice president's Milwaukee offensive targets not just visa cheats but the entire ecosystem Indian professionals navigate — from IT staffing firms to employment-based green cards. Immigration lawyers call it political theater. The diaspora is bracing for collateral damage.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Vice President Vance launched a major investigation into H-1B visa fraud targeting Indian professionals.
  • 73% of H-1B workers in the U.S. are from India, many holding advanced degrees.
  • Critics argue the fraud statistics may exaggerate the issue, conflating errors with criminal activity.
  • 40% of Indian Americans have considered leaving the U.S. due to political climate and safety concerns.
  • The investigation could impact the careers and lives of 600,000 H-1B holders.

## The Investigation Vice President JD Vance stood before a cheering crowd in Milwaukee on July 8 and announced what the Trump administration is calling the most significant crackdown on work-visa fraud in American history. The Department of Labor, he said, had already fired off dozens of subpoenas targeting employers and labor brokers suspected of gaming the H-1B visa system. "American jobs ought to go to American workers and not foreign fraudsters," Vance declared, flanked by Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito. "If you are trying to take advantage of that visa program, you are not allowed into the United States of America." The investigation's scope is sweeping. D'Esposito told reporters his office has already uncovered "widespread schemes in which employers and labor brokers submitted fraudulent applications, exploited foreign workers through coercive wage-kickback arrangements, and undercut American workers by flooding the market with below-wage labor." The probe extends beyond H-1B visas to PERM certifications — the permanent labor certifications that form the pathway to employment-based green cards — meaning the investigation could touch nearly every stage of the legal immigration pipeline that Indian professionals depend on. D'Esposito singled out the healthcare sector, claiming visa fraud has cost the medical industry "hundreds of millions" of dollars. He also named whistleblowers pointing to "some of the biggest companies," including Cognizant Technology Solutions, the India-founded IT services giant based in New Jersey that is already battling a False Claims Act suit in the Third Circuit over alleged H-1B fee evasion. Cognizant did not respond to requests for comment. ## The Numbers Behind the Alarm ![Vice President Vance — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/March_2026_Official_Vice_Presidential_Portrait_of_JD_Vance_%28head-and-shoulders_cropped%29.jpg) > **"D'Esposito singled out the healthcare sector, claiming visa fraud has cost the medical industry "hundreds of millions" of dollars."** The administration's central statistic — that Department of Homeland Security assessments have found as many as 21 percent of H-1B petitions to be fraudulent — sounds devastating. However, this figure, drawn from site-visit audits conducted years ago, has been widely disputed by immigration attorneys. Critics argue that the statistic may conflate minor documentation errors or technical violations with deliberate, criminal fraud, potentially inflating the perceived scale of the problem. Kelly Fortier, a partner at Michael Best who has handled H-1B cases for over two decades, pushed back sharply. "If Vice President Vance has concerns about this and if people are concerned about this, I guess I would like to see the evidence, because I personally have not seen it in my day-to-day practice," she told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. "I'm not surprised by the rhetoric, but I'm disappointed in it." Doris Brosnan, an employment attorney at von Briesen & Roper with 27 years of experience, echoed the skepticism. "I myself have not encountered any companies abusing the H-1B program," she said. "I can't say that there isn't any fraud. Of course, there's fraud. But the question is, how widespread is it, and what's the way to correct it?" Both attorneys noted that existing safeguards — worksite visits, prevailing wage requirements, actual wage comparisons — already function to catch fraud. "There are efforts in place and programs in place to catch this potential fraud, so it's not like it's just been ignored all these years," Fortier said. ## The Diaspora in the Crosshairs None of this unfolds in a vacuum. Seventy-three percent of all H-1B workers come from India, according to Pew Research. More than half hold master's degrees. They fill roles at Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Apple, and they are concentrated in precisely the coastal metros — California, New York, Washington State — where the investigation's subpoenas are most likely to land. For many NRIs, the H-1B visa is not just a work permit but a critical pathway to building a life, supporting families back home through remittances, and eventually achieving permanent residency or even dual citizenship. The timing compounds the anxiety. Just days before Vance's Milwaukee announcement, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma — an Indian American born in Wisconsin — announced 1,600 layoffs at Microsoft's gaming division. When the Federal Reserve then appointed Sharma to a new task force on productivity and jobs, the backlash turned explicitly racial. "Her one function is to purge white Americans and replace them with Indian cheap foreign labor," one widely shared post on X read. Sharma was born in the United States. ![Carnegie Endowment — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3d/Carnegie_Endowment_for_International_Peace_-_Dupont_Circle.JPG)
The Fraud Investigation's Scope
›Dozens of subpoenas issued targeting employers and labor brokers.
›Investigation includes both H-1B visas and PERM certifications.
›Healthcare sector reportedly lost hundreds of millions due to fraud.
›Cognizant Technology Solutions named in ongoing legal issues.
The H-1B probe and the Sharma episode are legally unrelated but culturally entangled. Together, they feed a narrative in which Indian professionals are cast simultaneously as the fraudsters exploiting the system and the executives dismantling American jobs — a double bind that leaves little room for the reality that most H-1B workers are highly skilled immigrants playing by the rules. This narrative can have a chilling effect on the Indian diaspora, impacting professional opportunities, social integration, and even family ties for those considering immigration or already living in the US. Meanwhile, the Carnegie Endowment's 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey, conducted between November 2025 and January 2026, found that 40 percent of Indian Americans have considered leaving the United States. Among those contemplating departure, 58 percent cited the political climate as the primary reason. Forty-one percent cited personal safety concerns. Nearly one-third reported avoiding political expression on social media, and one-fifth said they had stopped wearing Indian attire in public, all due to fear of discrimination. ## What Comes Next The investigation has no announced timeline. D'Esposito's office is pursuing leads from whistleblowers, and the subpoenas already issued suggest months of document review before any enforcement actions materialize. The probe also lands at a moment when the administration's other H-1B restrictions are faltering — a federal judge struck down Trump's proposed $100,000 annual fee for H-1B applicants in June, ruling it exceeded executive authority. For the Indian diaspora, the practical implications depend on where the investigation leads. If it surfaces genuine staffing-company fraud — shell employers, fake job postings, wage-kickback schemes — the crackdown could actually protect the legitimate H-1B workers who are often the victims of such arrangements. If it becomes a vehicle for broader immigration restriction under the banner of fraud prevention, the consequences for a community already questioning its place in America could be profound, affecting everything from career trajectories to the ability to maintain family connections across borders.
Impact on Indian Diaspora
›Investigation may affect professional opportunities for Indian workers.
›Concerns over discrimination and social integration are rising.
›Political rhetoric may create a chilling effect on the community.
›Potential for broader immigration restrictions under fraud prevention.
As Fortier put it: "The H-1B employers here in Wisconsin, I don't think they're going to appreciate hearing this because it almost paints a picture like they're doing something wrong or they shouldn't be using the program. But it's really important to them." For 600,000 H-1B holders and the millions more in the green card backlog, the message from Milwaukee is clear: the system they trusted to bring them to America is now the system being investigated. Whether the probe yields justice or just politics will determine whether the fraying dream holds.
